title: If Only…
intro: Zero, first, second, third and mixed conditionals. Pick the verb form that makes the “if” sentence work.

A2.q: If it ___ tomorrow, we'll stay home.
A2.why: “If” + present simple, then “will” for the result: first conditional. No “will” after “if”.

A2.q: If you heat water to 100°C, it ___.
A2.why: A fact that is always true (water at 100°C): zero conditional, present simple in both halves.

A2.q: If I ___ time, I'll help you.
A2.why: The result has “I’ll”, so the “if” half takes present simple: first conditional.

A2.q: If she studies hard, she ___ the exam.
A2.why: A possible future result of studying: first conditional, so “will pass”.

A2.q: Ice ___ if you leave it in the sun.
A2.why: What always happens to ice in the sun: zero conditional, present simple “melts”.

A2.q: If we don't hurry, we ___ the bus.
A2.why: A real danger in the future: first conditional, “if” + present, then “will miss”.

A2.q: If you touch fire, it ___ you.
A2.why: A general truth about fire: zero conditional, present simple with “-s” for “it”.
After “if”, use present simple for the future, even with an instruction (“call me”).

A2.q: Plants ___ if you don't water them.
A2.why: What always happens to plants: zero conditional, present simple “die” for the plural “plants”.

A2.q: If it's sunny tomorrow, we ___ to the beach.
A2.why: “Tomorrow” is a real future plan: first conditional, “will go”.

A2.q: If the stagecoach arrives late tonight, the sheriff ___ angry.
A2.why: “Tonight” is a real future possibility: first conditional, “will be”.

A2.q: If you ___ to Valencia in March, you'll see the Fallas.
A2.why: The result has “you’ll”, so the “if” half takes present simple, not “will”.

B1.q: If I ___ rich, I would travel the world.
B1.why: An imaginary situation now: second conditional, past form after “if”, with “were” after “I” in careful English.

B1.q: If she had more time, she ___ learn Italian.
B1.why: “If” + past simple (had) for an unreal present, then “would” for the result.

B1.q: What would you do if you ___ a lottery ticket?
B1.why: “What would you do…?” imagines something unlikely: past simple “won” after “if”.

B1.q: If I ___ you, I would apologise.
B1.why: The set phrase for advice is “If I were you”: second conditional.

B1.q: If he asked me, I ___ help him.
B1.why: “If he asked” is past simple for an imaginary situation, so the result takes “would”.

B1.q: They would move house if they ___ more money.
B1.why: “Would move” in the result means the “if” half takes past simple: “had”.

B1.q: If it weren't so cold, we ___ go for a walk.
B1.why: “If it weren’t” imagines a different present: second conditional, “would”.

B1.q: She would be happier if she ___ a new job.
B1.why: “Would be” in the result: past simple “got” after “if”, never “would” in that half.

B1.q: If you ___ me, what would you do?
B1.why: “If you were me” is the usual way to ask for advice; “was” does not go with “you”.

B1.q: We would visit more often if we ___ nearer.
B1.why: “Would visit” in the result: past simple “lived” after “if” for an unreal present.

B1.q: If the town ___ a doctor, the cowboys wouldn't have to ride for two days.
B1.why: “Wouldn’t have to” imagines a different present: past simple “had” after “if”.

B1.q: If I lived in Valencia, I ___ paella every Sunday.
B1.why: “If I lived” is an imaginary present, so the result takes “would eat”.

B2.q: If I had studied harder, I ___ passed the exam.
B2.why: “If I had studied” looks back at the past: third conditional, “would have passed”.

B2.q: She wouldn't have missed the flight if she ___ earlier.
B2.why: “Wouldn’t have missed” is about the past: the “if” half takes past perfect, “had left”.

B2.q: If they had known about the traffic, they ___ left earlier.
B2.why: “If they had known” is third conditional, so the result is “would have left”.

B2.q: I wouldn't have called you if it ___ urgent.
B2.why: “Wouldn’t have called” is a past result: past perfect in the “if” half, “hadn’t been”.

B2.q: If he ___ the map, we wouldn't have got lost.
B2.why: “Wouldn’t have got lost” is a past result: past perfect “had checked” after “if”.

B2.q: We would have arrived on time if the train ___ delayed.
B2.why: “Would have arrived” is third conditional: past perfect “hadn’t been” after “if”.

B2.q: If she had told me, I ___ come earlier.
B2.why: “If she had told me” is past perfect: the result is “would have come”.

B2.q: They wouldn't have won if the referee ___ that mistake.
B2.why: “Wouldn’t have won” is about a past match: past perfect “hadn’t made” after “if”.

B2.q: If I ___ there yesterday, I would have said something.
B2.why: “Yesterday” and “would have said” both point to the past: past perfect “had been”.

B2.q: You wouldn't have been late if you ___ up earlier.
B2.why: “Wouldn’t have been late” is a past result: past perfect “had got up” after “if”.

B2.q: If Fleming hadn't left his dishes out, he ___ penicillin.
B2.why: “Hadn’t left” looks back at 1928: third conditional, “wouldn’t have discovered”.

B2.q: The outlaws would have escaped if the sheriff ___ the bridge.
B2.why: “Would have escaped” is a past result: past perfect “hadn’t closed” after “if”.

C1.q: If she ___ harder at university, she would have a better job now.
C1.why: Past cause (university), present result (“now”): mixed conditional, past perfect after “if”.

C1.q: Were I in your position, I ___ accept the offer.
C1.why: “Were I” is a formal second conditional without “if”, so the result takes “would”.

C1.q: Had they invested earlier, they ___ much richer today.
C1.why: “Had they invested” is a past cause; “today” makes the result present: “would be”.

C1.q: If I hadn't missed that train, I ___ living in Paris now.
C1.why: Past cause (the train), present result (“now”): “would be living”.

C1.q: Should you need anything, ___ hesitate to call.
C1.why: “Should you need” is a polite first conditional, so the result can be a plain instruction: “don’t”.

C1.q: If it hadn't been for your help, I ___ never have finished.
C1.why: “If it hadn’t been for” is third conditional: “would never have finished”.

C1.q: Had it not been for the rain, the match ___ have been cancelled.
C1.why: “Had it not been for” + “wouldn't have been cancelled”: a third conditional without “if”; the rain is why it was cancelled.

C1.q: If she weren't so stubborn, she ___ have listened to advice.
C1.why: Present character (“weren’t so stubborn”), past result: mixed conditional, “would have listened”.

C1.q: Had I known the truth then, I ___ act differently now.
C1.why: Past cause (“had I known then”), present result (“now”): “would act”.

C1.q: If only I ___ that mistake — I regret it deeply.
C1.why: “If only” about a past regret takes past perfect: “hadn’t made”.

C1.q: Had Jenner not ___ the milkmaids, smallpox might have killed millions more.
C1.why: “Had … not” + past participle is a formal third conditional without “if”.

C1.q: If the railway hadn't come through, the town ___ a ghost town today.
C1.why: Past cause (the railway), present result (“today”): mixed conditional, “would be”.
